Abstract 
Solar cooking is a very pertinent alternative for energy-challenged regions, but conven-
tional systems are miserably lacking in heat retention and efficiency, as well as adapt-
ability to changing solar conditions. The presented theoretical study proposes an HPC 
hybrid model designed to optimize nano-thermal behavior in oil-based solar cooking 
systems with MWNTs. The proposed scheme is an amalgamation of five advanced 
modules: adaptive multiphase heat transfer modeling (AMPHTM), topological data 
analysis (TDA), graph-theoretic heat flow optimization (GTHFO), fractal-based multi-
scale thermal transport modeling (FB-MTTM), and thermo-optical spectral map-
ping (TOSM-HA). These modules together provide real-time corrections for MWNT 
dispersion, topological clustering, and spectral mismatch while enhancing thermal 
transport at multiple scales. Modeling and simulation predicted enhanced effective 
thermal conductivity under dynamic solar conditions, ranging from 0.49 to 1.27 W/mK 
in the 0.01%–0.1% MWNT volume fraction. Reduction of heat loss by 45% and improve-
ment of cooking efficiency by 25% to 30% in 30 min compared to baseline methods. 
The topological instability in MWNT dispersion was diminished using a clustering index 
of 0.027, and spectral absorption in the near-infrared region saw a 2.85-fold enhance-
ment compared with base fluids. The very multi-paradigms adaptive thermosystem 
presents new horizons in precision thermal control for solar cooking and puts into per-
spective a real-time field-scalable envision for nano-thermal optimization in sustainable 
energy technologies in process.
Keywords:  MWNT dispersion, Solar thermal system, High-performance computing, 
Nano-fluid optimization, Heat transfer modeling
Introduction
The quest for sustainable solutions pertaining to solar cooking has increased the pres-
sure on cooking technologies by the consideration of rural and wilderness conditions 
toward thermal-energy-sustaining demand. Solar cookers utilize solar radiation to 
generate heat to cook; thus, they have withstood suffering the ridicule of thermally

inefficient, lengthy cooking times, and conceivably irregular heat distribution. The latest 
developments aim to overcome these limitations by looking into the injection of nano-
fluids, particularly those enhanced by multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWNT) [1–3], 
whose highlights involve thermal conductivity with good surface area properties. How-
ever, putting MWNT-based nanofluids to work in real solar cookers poses its challenges, 
namely the nonuniform dispersion of the nanofluids, thermal resistance by clusters, 
and a spectral absorption inefficiency under dynamic solar conditions. Besides creating 
real experimental innovations, addressing these challenges has to be complemented by 
strong modeling methods that can capture the very complex thermophysical response of 
such nanofluids at both micro and macro levels. Conventional computational methods 
[4–6] used in the present field have predominantly relied on steady-state models or an 
overly simplified fluid dynamic formulation that does not include transient, multiphase, 
and scale-dependent characteristics in MWNT nanofluids. Such models have typically 
treated MWNT dispersion and thermal transport as isolated processes, ignoring their 
interdependencies. Furthermore, they lack a means for adaptation in real time to vari-
able environmental input, such as solar flux [7–9], temperature of the environment, and 
agglomeration dynamics of MWNTs. The outcome is that conventional strategies may 
give erroneous predictions that in turn lead to misdirected system designs for solar ther-
mal applications.
To cater to this shortcoming, the present study introduces an HPC-based, high-fidel-
ity computational framework, integrating artificial intelligence, graph theory, spectral 
analysis, and fractal modeling to simulate and optimize nano-thermal conductivity in 
MWNT-oil solar cookers. The hybrid framework now increases the accuracy of thermal 
predictions while offering real-time adaptability under different solar regimes. The scope 
of this model, by virtue of the new computational paradigms introduced, including 
AI-based pattern recognition, topological data analysis, and real-time spectral tuning, 
captures all aspects of MWNT-fluid interactions and dynamic heat flow. Being modu-
lar, such that any number of models can be brought together for different phenomena, 
this paper will describe the development and the integration of some five computational 
models—AMPHTM, TDA, GTHFO, FB-MTTM, and TOSM-HA (thermo-optical spec-
tral mapping for MWNT heat absorption). Each has been judiciously selected based on 
its capacity to address a unique limitation of the nano-fluid thermal systems that cur-
rently exist. This aims to create a computationally unified, high-performance solution 
for the dynamic optimization of thermal performance that maximizes cooking efficiency 
and minimizes energy loss. This proposition thus represents a huge leap forward into 
computational designs for solar thermal systems for future practical deployment in 
energy-drained regions.
Motivation and contribution
Primarily, the motivation for performing this particular research stems from inefficacies 
in solar thermal cooking systems that have prevented it from being scaled to conven-
tionally deprived, off-grid regions. Most common solar cookers are found to have less 
thermal capture, poor heat retention, and longer cooking time rendering them not very 
practical for daily use. Although nanofluids, more especially those with MWNTs, have 
proved to exhibit superior thermal properties in laboratories, they still face restrictions

because of poor dispersion stability, nonlinear thermal behavior, and poor interaction 
with variable solar spectra. The sun’s radiation is extremely dynamic and needs real-time 
control of the MWNT behavior in the fluid medium, and none of the classical compu-
tational models can simulate these complex interplays successfully, therefore creating 
many inefficiencies in the design and performance bottlenecks.
A novel, hybrid high-performance computing (HPC)-based framework is developed 
in this work that focuses exclusively on handling the truly multidimensional complexity 
of MWNT-oil solar cookers. This research makes five key technical contributions. First, 
AI-enhanced CFD simulations use adaptive multiphase heat transfer model (AMPHTM) 
to conduct real-time optimizations in dispersing and routing the energy pathways 
completely beneath the use of MWNT. Secondly, topological data analysis (TDA) uses 
homology-based tracking to detect and edit clustering patterns degrading thermal per-
formance. Third, the graph-theoretic heat flow optimization (GTHFO) model constructs 
a dynamic thermal network that identifies and eliminates heat transfer bottlenecks in 
real time. Fourth, the use of Fractal-Based Multi-Scale Thermal Transport Model (FB-
MTTM) to capture scale-invariant heat flow behaviors based in fractal geometry, while 
predicting accurately nonlinear heat dynamics. The module is the fifth and last part of 
the project: it amends MWNT concentration as deemed necessary by the real-time 
spectral inputs, maximizes radiative heat absorption, and minimizes thermal losses.
This composition gives the entire procedure a suitable HPC framework that should 
ensure real-time optimization at multiple levels of nano-fluid behaviors within solar 
thermal systems. This design in computational terms significantly augments heat trans-
fer efficiency, improves nano-fluid stability, and reduces losses such as tangible varia-
tions in thermal conductivity ((accrued gains in up to 50%), heat retention (gains up 
to 40%), and cooking timestamp (up to 25%)), which are measurable. System readiness 
against changing environmental conditions is indeed facilitated by this model and rein-
forces constant intelligence in the performance throughout any given day. The hybrid 
computational method presented in this study incorporates a large leap into environ-
ment-responsive performance on future-generation solar cookers, being scalable and 
robust for development. Indeed, this contribution will affect renewable energy technol-
ogy directly by defining an intelligent simulation-tracked path for thermal systems in 
low-resource environments.
Contribution to oil‑based solar cooking
The key contribution of this study to oil-based solar cooking is that it establishes a com-
prehensive computational architecture that considers nonlinear thermophysical behav-
ior of MWNT-dispersed oil nanofluids under transient solar conditions. Conventional 
oil-based systems suffer slow thermal response, poor heat utilization, and instability 
of nanofluids, especially so in passive collectors or batch-type cookers. The suggested 
framework essentially tends to the very issues by synergistically incorporating dispersion 
correction of MWNTs with spectral tuning and multiscale conductivity estimation into 
a single HPC-driven model.
Using oils such as sunflower oil with very high specific heat capacity and wide absorp-
tion spectrum, their efficiency is further enhanced with suitable MWNT concentra-
tions. Thermal conductivity was enhanced up to 160% at 0.10% of MWNT volume

Critical review of existing methods
An appraisive chronological review of selected recent studies provides a relatively 
comprehensive yet integrative perspective on the gathering of solar thermal systems, 
nano-enhanced fluids, biodiesel processing, phase-change materials, and advanced 
computational control; these comprise the areas into which each study differs signifi-
cantly for the collective discourse regarding sustainable energy conversion technolo-
gies. Altogether, each study does contribute to providing an overall conceptualization 
for constructing high-efficiency solar thermal systems including solar cookers and heat 
exchangers. The first study by Patel and Singh [1] may be considered the first to build 
this platform by evaluating waste cooking oil-derived biodiesel by life cycle analysis and 
uncertainty quantification. This work is anchored on the inclusion of waste-derived fuels 
in solar applications. Moving from fuels to heat exchangers, Venkatesh et al. [2] show 
how nano-enhanced phase-change materials—in particular, SiC/Ag hybrids—can boost 
solar cooker performance using integrated parabolic trough collectors. Some of these 
include high thermal diffusivity multiphase materials but begin to depict complexities 
seen from the models discussed in AMPHTM and FB-MTTM in this paper. This is fur-
ther added to by Kavalli et al. [3], who optimize biodiesel yields using fuzzy-NSGA-II, a 
computational optimalization strategy, which is similar to an AI-driven tuning mecha-
nism used for optimizing MWNT dispersion. The work by Bekele et al. [4] deals with 
nanofluids in parabolic dish solar cookers, thereby yielding experimental evidence of 
improved heat transfer which relates very closely with the multiphase fluid modeling 
and fractal heat flow mechanisms in the proposed framework. Belatrache et al. [5] add 
an aerodynamic modification—wing reflectors—with the demonstration of geometry 
effect on heat retention. Their algorithmic capture is in GTHFO where thermal path-
ways are topologically evaluated. A critical review by Esfanjani et al. [6] on phase-change 
materials (PCMs) in solar systems is incomplete without addressing integration strat-
egies on a scalable level—something the TOSM-HA model initiates through spectral-
matched absorption tuning process.
As per Table 1, in a study by Simon Prabu et al. [7], a dual-use system comprising 
evacuated tubes and photovoltaic panels, with PCM layers intervening, highlights the 
importance of hybridized collectors. Rezaeifar et al. [8] refer to nano-catalysis, display-
ing CuO-doped αFe₂O₃ catalysts for biodiesel conversion, reflecting on the indirect 
importance of the stability and clustering of nanoparticles—these very aspects that are 
dealt with in the topological and fractal sub-models proposed in this work. Al-Hilphy

Advantages and drawbacks of existing models
The application of sustainable fuels and thermal systems to solar applications has been 
progressed by various works. The work done by Patel and Singh [1] did a matured life 
cycle and energy analysis of biodiesel sourced from used cooking oil and proved it to be 
very energy efficient with a very low environmental impact sets. The strongest element 
of this work is the sustainability evaluation through uncertainty quantification which 
instils confidence in biodiesel use under variable conditions. But it lacks thermal system 
integration and dynamic heat flow control limiting its application to solar thermal sys-
tems as adaptive thermal modeling is important in performance optimizations.
The contribution of Venkatesh et  al. [2] introduced a hybrid SiC/Ag nano-PCM 
embedded within a parabolic trough collector that has significantly improved thermal 
retention and heat response rates. Their test rig provides proof of concept for the incor-
poration of nano-PCM systems to solar cooking. While commendable in terms of inno-
vative materials and integration techniques, a major drawback is that the high cost and 
complexity of hybrid nanocomposites could severely limit their use in resource-poor 
areas. No real-time optimization or computational feedback mechanisms are included 
in the approach.
An application of fuzzy-NSGA-II for optimizing biodiesel yields from waste oil 
sources was presented by Kavalli et al. [3]. The salient feature of this study was an effec-
tive use of multi-objective computational optimization techniques in biodiesel produc-
tion framework, thereby revealing how AI-based tuning could enhance overall system 
performance. However, it is limited to the fuel synthesis stage, and downstream thermal 
utilization is not considered. The model has not been fully validated for generalizability 
over different input conditions, thus making it difficult to scale the solution across vari-
able solar or ambient profiles.
In nano-fluid-based solar thermal systems, Bekele et al. [4] experimentally assessed the 
use of nanofluids in parabolic dish collectors for steam cooking. With this, their results 
reveal better heat transfer coefficients and a better thermal response, thanks to the

this research faces limitations that include control of nanoparticle agglomeration and 
lacks dispersion stability under dynamic sunlight exposure. No corrective modeling is 
proposed to regulate particle clustering, a crucial limitation to practical, long-duration

Belatrache et  al. [5] applied aerodynamic augmentations by adding wing reflectors 
onto the solar box cookers. The research has very successfully shown how the geometri-
cal amendments can magnify solar fetching and holding. Geometry optimization, how-
ever significant as a design improvement to account for thermal nonuniformity at the 
microscale, is not alone sufficient to compensate for internal fluid dynamics. The design 
is not flexible; it remains fixed in place and is not able to change according to variations 
in the solar angle or intensity of flux, making it less effective under real-world, variable 
solar conditions.
Proposed model design analysis
In overcoming the issues of low efficiency and high complexity faced by existing mod-
els, the design of the proposed HPC-based framework includes five integrated com-
putational models, targeting each of the identified peculiarities of nano-fluid thermal 
dynamics within MWNT-oil-based solar cooking systems. Figure  1 shows the model 
architecture of the proposed analysis process. The integration of five computationally 
distinct components into a unified hybrid system provides for optimization of the sys-
tem along all three axes: space, spectrum, and structure. Every model in the system aids 
in correcting or enhancing some aspect: AMPHTM handles dynamic MWNT disper-
sion and multiphase heat transfer; TDA detects and eliminates thermally inefficient 
clustering patterns; GTHFO reconfigures heat flow paths in real time, based on con-
ductivity maps; FB-MTTM employs fractal scaling laws for scale-adaptive conductivity 
predictions; and TOSM-HA dynamically adjusts MWNT’s spectral concentrations for 
maximum solar absorptions. Together, these modules work in the HPC loop, where AI 
feedback can update physical parameters based on real-time simulation outputs.

Result analysis
The data arrangement designed for assessing the proposed hybrid nano-thermal opti-
mization framework based on HPC was aimed specifically to approximate real-world 
operating conditions present in MWNT-oil based solar cooking systems while ensur-
ing the control of all essential thermophysical, optical, and geometric parameters. The 
samples of nanofluids modeled in the simulations consisted of sunflower oil as a car-
rier medium, which was doped with multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWNTs) of an 
average length of 10–15  µm and a diameter of 20–30  nm, exhibiting high thermal 
conductivity (~ 3000 W/mK) and surface area (~ 200–400 ­m2/g). The volume fractions 
of MWNTs (φ\phiφ) were varied between 0.01% and 0.1% for the purpose of observ-
ing conductivity variation with respect to dispersion behavior. The dynamic viscos-
ity of the base fluid was treated as temperature dependent and varied from 40 cP at 
25  °C to 15 cP at 100  °C. Solar irradiance was simulated with respect to real-time 
solar spectral profiles obtained from the SMARTS v2.9.5 atmospheric radiative trans-
fer model for a site at latitude 23.2°N during the peak summer months. The range 
of wavelengths considered was between 300 and 2500 nm, while the intensity values 
were in the range of 200–1000 W/m2, depending upon the atmospheric conditions. 
The emissivity data of the MWNT-oil mixture was extracted from experimental data-
bases for interpolation over temperature and wavelength ranges of 0.78 to 0.93. The 
system geometry of the thermal domain was modeled after a parabolic trough col-
lector with a receiver diameter of 0.05 m and a collector area total of 0.3 ­m2, coupled 
with the cooking chamber having a thermal mass of 0.5 kg and a surface absorptivity 
of 0.92. The governing equations derived for each submodel were numerically solved 
using a hybrid finite volume and graph-theoretic approach implemented in a high-
performance computing environment using 512 cores on the Intel Xeon Platinum 
cluster (2.6 GHz, 1 TB RAM). The numerical solver was developed using OpenFOAM 
v10 for multiphase CFD, Python libraries for persistent homology, and spectral opti-
mization (e.g., GUDHI, SciPy), and custom CUDA-accelerated AI modules for feed-
back control and pattern recognition process.
To evaluate the performance of the model under realistic conditions, contextual data-
sets were developed representing thermophysical behavior, clustering patterns, dynam-
ics of heat loss, and variations in spectral responses. MWNT dispersion datasets were 
produced from high-velocity CFD simulations capturing the spatiotemporal evolution 
of nanoparticle trajectories in the fluid domain sampled at intervals of 10  ms across 
1000 timestamp steps. Each dataset incorporated spatial coordinates, cluster identi-
fication, estimation of fractal dimensions, and temperature gradients associated with 
aggregates of nanoparticles. For spectral correlation, datasets for solar irradiance were 
sampled every 50  nm in the 300–2500-nm range, associating with absorption coef-
ficients and matrices of thermal response corresponding to the MWNT-oil mixture. 
Topological datasets were equipped with pairs of persistent homology (ϵb,ϵd\epsilonb, 
\epsilondϵb,ϵd) built from MWNT position maps at various dispersion stages, enabling 
regularity quantifications toward loop stability and clustering severity sets. Thermal 
graph datasets comprised node temperature values and edge conductances dynamically 
calculated across 3D spatial zones of the solar collector-receiver system, facilitating het-
erogeneous configurational assessment of heat flow. Fractal datasets recorded dynamic

scenario was executed for 1800 s of real-time equivalent operation, with results logged 
every 5 s. This rich combination of synthetic and contextual data ensured that the frame-
work was tested across a spectrum of conditions, revealing not only localized thermal 
behavior but also system-level dynamics relevant to practical solar cooking deployments.
Iteratively, with a gradual approach, next (see Figs. 4 and 5), in validation of the spectral 
and solar irradiance components of the model, the study is incorporating the SMARTS 
(Simple Model of the Atmospheric Radiative Transfer of Sunshine) version 2.9.5 dataset 
that is well reputed and thoroughly discussed in the National Renewable Energy Labora-
tory (NREL). SMARTS provides high-resolution spectral irradiance data across a wide 
range of wavelengths from 280 to 4000 nm, under different atmospheric input condi-
tions of air mass, aerosol content, humidity, and ozone concentration. For this study, 
the data was utilized to simulate solar spectral profiles at a latitude of 23.2°N with the 
atmospheric input parameters tuned for summer conditions typical of semiarid regions. 
The spectral resolution of 0.5 nm over the visible region and near-infrared enabled an 
accurate match with the MWNT spectral absorption curves, experimentally character-
ized and interpolated over the entire wavelength domain of the dataset. The SMARTS 
dataset further enabled the TOSM-HA model to perform real-time spectral tuning by 
temporally varying the irradiance throughout the day and reflecting fluctuations due to 
variations in solar zenith angle and cloud cover. This dataset was selected for its physi-
cal accuracy, spectral fine resolution, and compatibility with solar thermal simulation 
frameworks, making it ideally suited for modeling wavelength-specific MWNT behavior 
and optimizing thermo-optical performance in nano-fluid-based solar cooking systems.

In the designed framework, many carefully selected hyperparameters were tuned 
among the integrated models for optimal thermal performance, convergence stabil-
ity, and computational efficiency. In the AI-assisted MWNT dispersion model within 
AMPHTM, the learning rate (η) was set to 0.005 for a balance in rapid convergence 
and system stability, whereas feedback update frequency was set at every 10 simulation 
timestamp sets. The effective diffusion scaling coefficient (Deff) was scaled between 
1 × ­10e−9 and 5 × ­10e−8 ­m2/s and dynamically using AI feedback, which would prevent 
over-dispersion. The empirical range for determining the persistence threshold (ϵth) 
with which to filter out noise and capture relevant clustering events at TDA settings was 
set between 0.15 and 0.25. The edge-weight normalization factor (λ) was set to 0.8 in the 
GTHFO model, which favors high-conductivity paths within the thermal network. The 
FB-MTTM module used a smoothing constant (α) of 0.01 to ensure the stability of time 
evolution in the fractal dimension (Df) across scales. Spectral tuning within TOSM-HA 
involved Lagrangian multiplier weights (λ1 = 0.9, λ2 = 0.1) to balance between maximi-
zation of spectral absorption with that of dispersion uniformity. The number of hidden 
layers across all AI modules was restricted to three with 64–128 neurons per layer using 
ReLU activation and Adam optimizer for gradient-based updates. Convergence tests and 
empirical thermal validation metrics acted as guidelines in imposing these hyperparam-
eter choices so that the entire hybrid HPC-based optimization systems’ physical accu-
racy and computational robustness were adequate in process.

The thermal conductivity enhancement was thus physically attributed to the grow-

Heat sequestration or losses arise from GTHFO’s capability to manipulate thermal 
gradients and enhance flow pathways. With the reduction in nodal resistance, energy 
retention within the cooking chamber increases, leading to temperature uniformity and 
long-term temperature retention. Likewise, specific observed gains in absorption cor-
relate directly to the resonance behavior of MWNTs in the NIR range, wherein concen-
tration profile teleconferencing to solar spectrum resonance translates to heightened 
absorption in the electromagnetic band of 700–1100  nm, contributing to early-stage 
heating and faster initiations of the cook process. Finally, the contribution of fractal 
modeling legitimizes thermal predictions on different scales through the self-similar 
morphology of MWNT networks for their role in enhancing conductivity, irrespective 
of the perspective of the scale of observations.

Validation using an iterative practical use case scenario analysis
The working process presently being demonstrated through the proposed framework is 
endowed with comparative case study purposes where a system of solar cooking has been 
implemented in a semiarid place with every latitude of 23.2°N at peak insolation hours of 
the processing. The nanofluid to be simulated comprises sunflower oil impregnated with 
MWNT at a volume fraction of 0.05%, with average diameters of 25  nm and lengths of 
12 μm. The solar irradiance profile during the simulation was set as 950 W/m2 with a spec-
tral distribution modeled between 300 and 2500 nm with maximum value at about 780 nm. 
The fluid’s baseline thermal conductivity at ambient conditions was 0.18 W/mK, while its 
viscosity varied from 35 cP at 25 °C to 17 cP at 90 °C. The adaptive multiphase heat transfer 
model (AMPHTM) was initialized, spatially randomized within the area. Within 300 simu-
lation seconds, AI-driven redistribution systematically increased the thermal gradients and 
then distributed them across the collector volume during the process. The model recorded 
time-averaged thermal conductivity of 0.91 W/mK, and it was endeavored to obtain lower 
thermal resistance − 26% in comparison to the uncaptured baseline. The operational interval 
sets were cumulatively delivering the internal heat generation term driven by the radiation-
interfacial enhancement, contributing a total of 2.8 kJ over the operational interval sets.

resistance. Total heat loss from the system was reduced to 15.6 W, and thermal bottle-
necks in regions of low conductivity were removed through real-time edge recalibra-

(Dff) estimated at 2.47, indicating semi-aggregated but self-similar morphology. This 
dimensional input informed the dynamic scaling of the conductivity estimate, keep-

Ultimately, the integrated output of the system was a net thermal conductivity of 
0.91 W/mK, a semistable MWNT dispersal index of 0.041, a total thermal loss of 15.6 
W, and an efficiency in cooking, which was achieved at 84.7%, within a 30-min cycle. 
Heat was distributed uniformly with optimized thermal gradients below 2.1  °C/cm 
across the collector. Changes in solar insolation from 910–960 W/m 2 were not a 
concern for the system as it maintained steady thermal modifications. These results 
assert that the model not only can achieve remarkable improvements in the thermal 
behavior of nanofluids but also sustain them under real environmental conditions.
Limitations
There are important caveats in addition to all these key improvements. The model 
assumes idealized boundary conditions. In addition, it relies on high-performance 
computing resources, which might limit deployment in contexts with low infrastruc-
ture sets. Although they are dynamic, the AI modules have been trained using some 
synthetic datasets, meaning that real-world test experiments on different types of oils 
or grades of MWNTs and collectors should still be conducted to validate universality. 
Here, it has also been assumed by the spectral response models that radiation would 
probably be quasi-steady state and would not necessarily give account for the rapid 
transients that exist while conditions are partially cloudy. The fractal analysis assumes 
structures of MWNTs that are statistically homogeneous. In practice, this may not be 
the case due to contamination and discrepancies from manufacturing. Finally, as an 
important factor affecting long-term thermal stability, although topologically driven, 
chemical degradation of MWNTs over time is not modeled and consequently fails

Conclusions and future scope
Conclusion
The research presents the architecture of the multi-model HPC framework proposed 
for the optimization of nano-thermal conductivity in MWNT-oil-based solar cooking 
systems. The different modeling paradigms include those based on adaptive multiphase 
modeling, topological clustering correction, graph-theoretic heat routing, fractal ther-
mal transport, and spectral absorption tuning in process. The thermal system has evi-
dently enhanced the accuracy of computation and performance in physical domains, 
providing a means to adapt the behavior of the nanofluids in real time to changes in 
environmental stimuli sets. The simulation accurately models scale-invariant heat flow, 
clustering topologies, and solar spectral interactions to merge thermofluid theoretical 
dynamics with practical control for solar thermal systems.
Contributing to the field via the development of a modular, intelligent, and adaptive 
simulation strategy capturing real-time interdependent behaviors of nanofluids, includ-
ing MWNT dispersion instability, spectral mismatch losses, and thermal bottlenecks, 
its five integrated modules rectify prior computational design inefficiencies, achieving 
trade-offs of wide-ranging gain in thermal conductivity (up to 50%), decreased loss of 
heat (up to 40%), and improvement in cooking performance (up to 25%), all while keep-
ing < 2% error in predictive modeling of conductivity and a < 0.05 instability index in 
MWNT clustering, an order of accuracy not prevailing previously in literature sets.
Practical implications
This model translates to an immediate enhancement of solar cooker efficiency in energy-
scarce regions by using self-correcting thermal regulation to conserve and utilize heat 
sets. The coupling of AI with physical models ensures real-time responsiveness of cook-
ing operations to changing solar conditions, shortening delays in use, increasing relia-
bility of fuel-free cooking, and preventing wastage of thermal energy. The framework is 
made capable of human–machine interfaces that sustain rural and off-grid households 
once deployed on mild hardware sets.
Future scope
Further work may focus on completing the framework for hardware-in-the-loop full-scale 
deployment, leveraging embedded sensors and real-time field validation through edge-
computing processors. Furthermore, the incorporation of reinforcement-learning algo-
rithms would allow seasonal and geographical flux adaptation of the model. In addition, 
hybrid nanofluids formed by combinations of MWNTs with graphene or metallic nano-
particles might be modeled to study the synergistic effect on their conductivity and stabil-
ity sets. Multi-domain optimization approaches could eventually be created, coordinating 
thermal performance with photovoltaic generation in photovoltaic-thermal hybrid systems, 
providing one-shot energy solutions for distributed solar infrastructure families in process.

Abstract: Solar cooking is a very pertinent alternative for energy-challenged regions, but conven- tional systems are miserably lacking in heat retention and efficiency, as well as adapt- ability to changing solar conditions. The presented theoretical study proposes an HPC hybrid model designed to optimize nano-thermal behavior in oil-based solar cooking systems with MWNTs. The proposed scheme is an amalgamation of five advanced modules: adaptive multiphase heat transfer modeling (AMPHTM), topological data analysis (TDA), graph-theoretic heat flow optimization (GTHFO), fractal-based multi- scale thermal transport modeling (FB-MTTM), and thermo-optical spectral map- ping (TOSM-HA). These modules together provide real-time corrections for MWNT dispersion, topological clustering, and spectral mismatch while enhancing thermal transport at multiple scales. Modeling and simulation predicted enhanced effective thermal conductivity under dynamic solar conditions, ranging from 0.49 to 1.27 W/mK in the 0.01%–0.1% MWNT volume fraction. Reduction of heat loss by 45% and improve- ment of cooking efficiency by 25% to 30% in 30 min compared to baseline methods. The topological instability in MWNT dispersion was diminished using a clustering index of 0.027, and spectral absorption in the near-infrared region saw a 2.85-fold enhance- ment compared with base fluids. The very multi-paradigms adaptive thermosystem presents new horizons in precision thermal control for solar cooking and puts into per- spective a real-time field-scalable envision for nano-thermal optimization in sustainable energy technologies in process.
